newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China exalts, HK ponders handover in 100 days.
newsitem.headline: China exalts, HK ponders handover in 100 days.

text.p: A grey drizzle blanketed Hong Kong on Sunday as the British colony marked the 100-day countdown to the handover to China but there were few signs that gloom would cast a pall over the final days of colonial rule.

For thousands, the day marked a glorious moment in the transition to reunification with the motherland at midnight on June 30, which they celebrated by parading through the streets to the ear-shattering clash of cymbals and kettle drums.

Far to the north of Hong Kong, hundreds of Beijing residents checked off the seconds as the digital clock in the Chinese capital's Tiananmen Square flashed down to midnight and the 100-day mark for the recovery of Hong Kong.
"We have endured 100 years of shame, 100 years of resistance and 100 years of waiting," said China's Guangming Daily. "Now in another 100 days, the hopes of generations will be realised."

In Hong Kong, more than seven thousand people took to the streets in a patriotic fervour, but for the vast majority of Hong Kong's 6.4 million hardworking populace, it was just another Sunday, a welcome day off for a community which works a five-and-a-half day week.

A stone's throw away from the procession of traditional dragon and lion dancers and celebrants waving a sea of red Chinese flags, thousands of residents indulged in the ritualistic orgy of beer-fuelled hedonism that has built up around the annual international Rugby seven-a-side tournament.
The tournament was honoured this year, the last under British rule, when Rugby Authorities made it into a world cup event and fans celebrated with gusto.
With just 100 days to go to a monumental change, Hong Kong is awash in conflicting emotions.

Some, like the street revellers, are delighted that China's humiliation at the hands of a foreign power is about to end. "This is a grand and great occasion. In just 100 days, we will return to the Chinese motherland," said chief organiser Raymond Wu.

The celebrants gathered in Victoria Park, named after the queen who reigned when Britain, at the height of its imperial powers, wrested Hong Kong from China's weak and crumbling Qing dynasty in the mid-19th century.

Others, particularly members of Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp, fret about their future under a China which has already put in place plans to dilute civil liberties and dissolve the elected legislative council, undoing democratic reforms spearheaded by the 28th and last British Governor, Chris Patten.

A handful of demonstrators, their mouths taped shut in what they said was a symbol of things to come, took up position in Victoria Park waving placards to silently condemn China's brutal military crackdown around Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Another small group of human rights activists marked the countdown with a street drama on Sunday voicing fears about the future after the handover on June 30.
Many Hong Kongers are keeping their fingers crossed that the handover will pass uneventfully and life will go on as usual.
Up to half a million have taken out insurance in the form of a foreign passport -- just in case. Nearly 50 percent plan to leave if things go wrong, opinion polls show.

But Hong Kong, as it enters the last leg of its drawn out transition from British colony to Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, has defied those who forecast a society in chaos, of panic, economic collapse and of deserted streets and boarded up buildings.
Business is booming and Hong Kong approaches the change with reserves in excess of HK$330 billion ($42.7 billion) in hand.

Patten, who said Hong Kong had reached this moment in its history in first class condition, nevertheless warned that rolling back freedoms and instituting a more authoritarian form of government threatened to damage the fragile mechanism.
"Hong Kong is, as I said recently, a smoothly functioning community. It's like a Rolls Royce," Patten said in a Radio Hong Kong broadcast.
"All you need to do if you're in charge is to slip into the driving seat, switch on the ignition and away you go.

"I don't quite see the point of lifting the bonnet to tinker with the engine. That only raises worries about whether it will work so well, and whether you may be persuaded by some people to start stripping it down for spare parts."

China's envoy to Hong Kong, Zhou Nan, brushed aside these concerns and urged Hong Kong people to unite around future leader Tung Chee-hwa, a 59-year-old shipping magnate anointed by Beijing in December to step into Patten's shoes.

Tung, a conservative businessman, has endorsed China's plans for clipping key civil liberties clauses in the law. He argues the changes are technicalities and will not materially affect Hong Kong's freedoms.

"The central government places great trust in the future Hong Kong SAR government. I think all sectors in Hong Kong should give their full support," China's Zhou said in an interview with Hong Kong-based Cable Television.
